source.journal_name: Romanian Journal of Information Science and Technology

paper.title: Nurse and Paramedic Rostering with Constraint Programming: A Case Study
paper.abstract: Paraphrase: a real case study of nurse rostering for mid-size Chilean hospitals that roster by hand under the uncommon "fourth shift" system, modelled with constraint programming as a classic model and as a model based on global constraints, both intended to apply to any fourth-shift health care centre.

artifact_assessment.evidence: no availability statement or link in the text

flag_details.FORMALISM_THEATER: Level 2 paper with three formal elements that fail the Necessity Test (Q1 yes, Q2 no, Q3 no): the definition of a CSP as a triple P = ⟨X, D, C⟩ of variable, domain and constraint tuples, the definition of a CSP solution as an assignment {x1 → a1, …, xn → an}, and the definition of a DFA as M = (Q, Σ, δ, q0, F). None is used by the model, the experiments or any argument; the constraint formulas of the model itself pass the test.
flag_details.DECORATIVE_DEFINITIONS: The same three inline tuple definitions are formal definitions of standard concepts, each replaceable by one plain sentence; removing them would not change what a programmer builds, and no proof refers to them (the paper has none). The automaton the paper actually passes to regular does not satisfy its own DFA definition: it has two transitions on 0 from states 1 and 5 and two on 1 from state 7.
flag_details.EXCESSIVE_SELF_CITATION: SCR = 11/28 = 39.3% (above 30%): references [8]-[12], [18], [19] and [23]-[26] include at least one of the five authors. Eight of them ([8]-[12], [18], [25], [26]) are cited only in the closing future-work sentence, with [10] listed twice in one bracket; no self-citation falls below 0.3 similarity.
flag_details.NO_LIMITATIONS: No limitations section and no acknowledgment of constraints on the results. The only candidate, a closing remark that the solution is ongoing work and could be extended to bigger centres, is a future-work pointer; the runtime-only evaluation, the unvalidated rosters and the single-centre preference examples go unmentioned.

verdict.summary: Level 2 constraint-programming case study of fourth-shift nurse rostering whose constraint model is proportionate, but whose textbook tuple definitions of a CSP, its solutions and a DFA do no work. Eleven of 28 references are self-citations, eight stacked on one future-work sentence; the evaluation reports runtimes only, the printed chief-nurse constraints contain errors, no limitations are stated and nothing is released.

papers.provenance:
## Formalism Analysis

### Concept Complexity
**Topic:** Case study of rostering for nurses, paramedics and chief nurses in six mid-size Chilean health care centres that use the two-shift "fourth shift" cycle (day, night, off, off). The problem is modelled as a constraint satisfaction problem in two variants, reified implications with occurrences constraints and a regular constraint over an automaton for the cycle, solved in ECLiPSe and timed under six variable/value-ordering heuristics.
**Level:** 2 (Low)
**Rationale:** The contribution is a constraint model of one rostering problem, assembled from standard modelling devices (implications over finite-domain variables, the occurrences and regular global constraints) and solved by an existing solver. The experiments only time six instance sizes under six enumeration strategies. That is an existing technique applied to a new domain, plus a configuration comparison, which the specification places at Level 2. There is no new algorithm, complexity analysis or proof that would justify Level 3. The modelling work is more than an API integration, so Level 1 would understate it.

### Formal Elements
- Definitions: 3 (with constraints: 0; none of the three constrains the implemented model). Only statements that define a concept count here: a CSP, a CSP solution and a DFA. Variable declarations and the column shorthands V_j and X_j are inventoried with the model statements.
- Theorems: 0
- Proofs: 0
- Equations: 31 distinct formal statements of the model, plus 9 restatements in Section 4. The 31 are 3 variable domains, 2 column shorthands, 22 constraints, the occurrences and regular constraint forms, the set of four regular expressions, and the automaton passed to regular. Algorithm 1, a generic backtracking/propagation loop, is pseudocode and is not counted.

### Necessity Test
Each model statement is posted to the ECLiPSe model or declares part of it, so removing it changes the rosters the solver accepts (Q2 yes). The three definitions describe the CSP and DFA formalisms in general and leave the implemented model untouched (Q2 no). No element carries a proof or bound, so Q3 is no throughout.
- Def., Sec. 2, CSP as a triple P = ⟨X, D, C⟩ of variable, domain and constraint tuples, each constraint a subset of a Cartesian product of domains: Q1 yes, Q2 no, Q3 no → unnecessary
- Def., Sec. 2, CSP solution as an assignment {x1 → a1, …, xn → an} with ai ∈ di and (aj1, …, ajnj) ∈ cj: Q1 yes, Q2 no, Q3 no → unnecessary
- Def., Sec. 4, DFA M = (Q, Σ, δ, q0, F) with δ : Q × V → Q and F ⊆ Q: Q1 yes, Q2 no, Q3 no → unnecessary
- Nurse domain V_{i,j} ∈ {0, 1, 2}: Q1 yes, Q2 yes, Q3 no → necessary
- Nurse constraint 1, V_{i,j} = 1 ⇒ V_{i,j+1} = 2: Q1 yes, Q2 yes, Q3 no → necessary
- Nurse constraint 2, V_{i,j} = 2 ⇒ V_{i,j+1} = 0: Q1 yes, Q2 yes, Q3 no → necessary
- Nurse constraint 3, (V_{i,j} = 0 ∧ V_{i,j+1} = 0) ⇒ V_{i,j+2} = 1: Q1 yes, Q2 yes, Q3 no → necessary
- Nurse constraint 4, V_{i,j} = 2 ⇒ (V_{i,j+1} = 0 ∧ V_{i,j+2} = 0): Q1 yes, Q2 yes, Q3 no → necessary
- Constraint form occurrences(Value, Vars, N): Q1 yes, Q2 yes, Q3 no → necessary
- Column shorthand V_j = {V_{1,j}, …, V_{nurses,j}}: Q1 yes, Q2 yes, Q3 no → necessary
- Nurse constraint 5, occurrences(0, V_j, nurses/2): Q1 yes, Q2 yes, Q3 no → necessary
- Nurse constraint 6, occurrences(1, V_j, nurses/4): Q1 yes, Q2 yes, Q3 no → necessary
- Nurse constraint 7, occurrences(2, V_j, nurses/4): Q1 yes, Q2 yes, Q3 no → necessary
- Nurse constraint 8, V_{3,1} ≠ 0: Q1 yes, Q2 yes, Q3 no → necessary
- Nurse constraint 9, V_{6,1} = 1 ∧ V_{12,1} = 1: Q1 yes, Q2 yes, Q3 no → necessary
- Nurse constraint 10, V_{10,20} = 0 ∧ V_{10,21} = 0: Q1 yes, Q2 yes, Q3 no → necessary
- Nurse constraint 11, V_{11,13} = 0 ∧ V_{11,14} = 0: Q1 yes, Q2 yes, Q3 no → necessary
- Nurse constraint 12, V_{13,7} = 0 ∧ V_{13,14} = 0: Q1 yes, Q2 yes, Q3 no → necessary
- Nurse constraint 13, V_{15,1} = 0 ∧ V_{15,2} = 0: Q1 yes, Q2 yes, Q3 no → necessary

- Paramedic constraint 1, P_{3,1} ≠ 0: Q1 yes, Q2 yes, Q3 no → necessary
- Paramedic constraint 2, P_{6,20} = 0 ∧ P_{6,21} = 0: Q1 yes, Q2 yes, Q3 no → necessary
- Paramedic constraint 3, P_{8,13} = 0 ∧ P_{8,14} = 0: Q1 yes, Q2 yes, Q3 no → necessary

- Chief-nurse constraint 2, the mirror case N > D with occurrences(1, X_j, S) ⇒ S = N − D: Q1 yes, Q2 yes, Q3 no → necessary

- Chief-nurse constraint 5, (occurrences(1, X_j, 4) ∨ occurrences(2, X_j, 3)) ∧ occurrences(0, X_j, 2): Q1 yes, Q2 yes, Q3 no → necessary
- Constraint form regular(δ, q0, F, X): Q1 yes, Q2 yes, Q3 no → necessary
- Regular expressions (0012)+, (0120)+, (1200)+, (2001)+: Q1 yes, Q2 yes, Q3 no → necessary
- Automaton instance regular([[0,1,2], …, [2,8,5]], 1, [5,6,7,8], X), 13 transitions: Q1 no, Q2 yes, Q3 no → necessary
- Section 4 restatements of nurse constraints 5-13 (nine formulas, the last printed with V_{15,4} in place of V_{15,1}): Q1 yes, Q2 yes, Q3 no → necessary (the same elements as above)

### Proportionality
Calculated complexity: 6 (3 definitions × 2; equations carry no weight in the formula)
Expected range (Level 2): 0-15
Ratio: 0.4x upper bound

**Assessment:** Proportionate in quantity. The constraint formulas are the model itself, written in the ordinary notation of constraint programming, and the solver enforces every one of them. The problem is not volume. It is the three textbook definitions, which fail the Necessity Test.

### Issues
- Section 2 restates the textbook CSP formalism: the triple and the definition of a solution. No later statement relies on either. Algorithm 1 names C and D as inputs, but it is itself generic background, not the ECLiPSe search the authors ran. One plain sentence would replace each definition without loss. At Level 2 this is the specification's pattern of formal definitions for data structures.
- The DFA 5-tuple in Section 4 is just as generic, and the paper's own automaton does not satisfy it. δ is typed over V instead of Σ. The automaton passed to regular is not deterministic: two transitions on 0 leave state 1 (to 2 and 3) and two leave state 5 (to 6 and 2), and two transitions on 1 leave state 7 (to 8 and 4). The cross-reference to the automaton's figure is broken in the text.
- The printed chief-nurse constraints match neither the text nor the instances:
  - Constraints 1-2 count day shifts (value 1) as N and night shifts (value 2) as D, the reverse of the shift labels. Nurse constraints 6-7 fix both counts at nurses/4, so the antecedents N < D and N > D can never hold and the two constraints never act.
  - Constraint 3 asks for nurses/2 chief nurses on one shift. For the 16N+16P+4CN instance that is eight, but the instance has only four chief nurses.
  - Constraint 5 is described as a weekly rule but is posted on the daily column X_j. There it needs two off values plus four day or three night values among those same four variables.
  - Constraint 4 forces an off day after three day shifts, which is stricter than the rule stated in words.

  As printed, the model could not produce the rosters reported for the smallest instance.
- Set notation is limited to index ranges, variable domains and the column lists V_j and X_j. The paper itself calls the argument of occurrences a list. No set operation stands in for a list operation, so UNNECESSARY_SET_THEORY is not raised.

---

## Citation Analysis

Eleven of the 28 references include at least one of the five authors: [8]-[12], [18], [19] and [23]-[26]. That gives SCR = 39.3%. Counted by in-text citation instance it is 12 of 30 (40%).

- Clearly related (similarity about 0.85-0.95): [19], the conference version this paper extends; [23] and [24], the authors' nurse-rostering models with soft and reified constraints, cited among the CP approaches.
- Marginal (about 0.3-0.5):
  - [8], [9], [10], [12] and [25], on autonomous search and enumeration-strategy selection in CP.
  - [11], on PSO tuning of a choice-function hyperheuristic for that selection.
  - [18], on a reactive hybrid constraint solver.
  - [26], on manufacturing cell formation with CP and SAT, cited for combining CP and SAT.

Each of the eight marginal works is cited once, and all in the closing sentence on future work: first [26], then the bracket [11, 18, 25, 10, 12, 10, 9, 8], which lists [10] twice. They support no claim the paper makes. None falls below 0.3, so IRRELEVANT_SELF_CITATION is not raised, but the ratio is well above the 30% threshold.

The other references cover the mathematical-programming, metaheuristic and CP literature on nurse rostering adequately. No mutual-citation pattern can be established from this paper alone.

---

## Structural Analysis

The body contains about 28 claim sentences. Twelve are backed by citations or by Table 1 and three partly, so CER ≈ 0.48 (weak).

The literature review and the runtimes are supported. Several claims are not:
- The problem framing: commercial tools fail hospitals' needs, and manual rostering is slow and error-prone.
- The fourth shift is called very uncommon and also said to be used in most Chilean hospitals, with no source for either.
- Rostering is said to take seconds where manual rostering takes days, but the manual effort is never measured.
- The conclusion says the models adapt easily to any fourth-shift hospital and assign shifts correctly.

The evaluation times six synthetic instance sizes under six heuristics, and nothing more:
- No comparison with the hospitals' manual rosters or with another method.
- No check of the rosters produced.
- Preferences are illustrated for a single centre.

The runtimes quoted in the text are those of the best strategies. First-fail with min value ordering takes about 120 s at 288 workers and times out at 576.

There is no limitations section. The only candidate is a closing remark that the solution is still ongoing work and could be extended to bigger centres. That points to future work and acknowledges no constraint on the reported results.

Artifacts: the paper links no code, model files or instances and makes no availability claim. The models are printed in the text, and ECLiPSe is a third-party solver.

---

## Conclusion

A modest application paper. It brings standard constraint programming modelling to an uncommon two-shift cycle for six hospitals and adds a second model built on the regular constraint. Its formulas are proportionate and are the substance of the contribution. But Sections 2 and 4 open with textbook tuple definitions of a CSP, its solutions and a DFA that do no work in the paper. Under the specification's zero-tolerance rule for Levels 1-2 that is formalism theater, if a mild case of it. Separately, and with more weight, 39% of the references are the authors' own, and eight of them are stacked on a single future-work sentence. That flag disqualifies at any concept level.

Beyond the flags, the evidence is thin:
- Only solver runtimes are reported.
- As printed, the chief-nurse constraints contain errors that would make the smallest instance infeasible.
- No limitation is acknowledged.
- Nothing is released for reproduction.

To serve as a reusable case study, the paper would need corrected constraints, rosters validated against the hospitals' requirements, and a public model.
